content: Jumping from a height, while not a common method of suicide, is highly lethal. Restricting access to means of suicide is a critical population-based strategy for suicide prevention, with strong evidence supporting its effectiveness. However, the specific evidence for restricting access to jumping sites as a means of suicide prevention is not well-established. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of interventions aimed at limiting access to means of suicide by jumping. These interventions include the installation of physical barriers, fencing, or safety nets at frequently used jumping sites, as well as measures to restrict access to these sites, such as road closures. To conduct this review, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Library, Embase, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and Web of Science, up to May 2019. Additional searches were conducted in international trial registries, such as the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) and ClinicalTrials.gov, to identify unpublished or ongoing studies. Reference lists of included studies and relevant systematic reviews were also examined, and authors and subject experts were contacted for further information. No restrictions were applied regarding the date, language, or publication status of the studies. Two independent reviewers assessed all citations to identify relevant studies, focusing on outcomes such as suicide, attempted suicide, self-harm, and cost-effectiveness of interventions. Eligible studies included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials, controlled intervention studies without randomization, before-and-after studies, and studies using interrupted time series designs. These studies evaluated interventions aimed at restricting access to means of suicide by jumping. Two reviewers independently selected studies for inclusion, and three reviewers extracted data. Studies with similar interventions and outcomes were pooled using random-effects meta-analysis, while data from other studies were synthesized narratively. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 14 studies were included in the review. Thirteen were before-and-after studies, and one was a cost-effectiveness analysis. Three studies each were conducted in Switzerland and the USA, while two studies each were from the UK, Canada, New Zealand, and Australia. Most studies (10 out of 14) evaluated jumping means restriction interventions implemented in isolation, with half of these interventions occurring at bridges. None of the studies included comparator interventions or control conditions due to their observational nature. During the pre-intervention period across the 13 before-and-after studies, there were 742.3 suicides (5.5 suicides per year) over 134.5 study years. In the post-intervention period, there were 70.6 suicides (0.8 suicides per year) over 92.4 study years, representing a 91% reduction in suicides. A meta-analysis of all studies assessing jumping means restriction interventions (whether implemented alone or in combination with other measures) demonstrated a significant reduction in suicides at intervention sites (12 studies; incidence rate ratio [IRR] = 0.09, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.03 to 0.27; P < 0.001; I² = 88.40%). Similar findings were observed in studies evaluating interventions implemented in isolation (9 studies; IRR = 0.05, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.16; P < 0.001; I² = 73.67%), as well as those combining jumping means restriction with other interventions (3 studies; IRR = 0.54, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.93; P = 0.03; I² = 40.8%). Studies assessing the effectiveness of physical barriers (7 studies; IRR = 0.07, 95% CI 0.02 to 0.24; P < 0.001; I² = 84.07%) and safety nets (2 studies; IRR = 0.09, 95% CI 0.01 to 1.30; P = 0.07; I² = 29.3%) also showed reductions in suicides. However, data on suicide attempts were limited, and none of the studies used self-harm as an outcome. There was significant heterogeneity in the primary outcome (suicide) across most analyses, except for those involving combined interventions and safety nets. Despite this, all studies included in the meta-analyses showed consistent directional effects favoring jumping means restriction interventions. Due to methodological limitations, the quality of evidence was rated as low. A cost-effectiveness analysis indicated that constructing physical barriers on bridges would be a highly cost-effective intervention in the long term, given the overall reduction in suicide mortality. In conclusion, the findings suggest that interventions to restrict access to means of suicide by jumping can significantly reduce the frequency of suicides at these sites. However, the evidence is of low quality due to methodological limitations. Further high-quality studies are needed to better evaluate the effectiveness of these interventions and explore other measures at jumping sites. Additionally, future research should investigate the potential for substitution of suicide methods and displacement effects in populations exposed to these interventions.
